validated_results.title: Alcohol consumption and risk of prostate cancer: The Harvard Alumni Health Study.
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort of Harvard alumni reporting multivariate relative risks for alcohol consumption and incident prostate cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: 1 to <3 drinks/day versus almost never drinking alcohol

sample_size.excerpt: We prospectively followed 7612 Harvard alumni (mean age 66.6 years) from 1988 through 1993, during which 366 cases of incident prostate cancer occurred.

cases.excerpt: We prospectively followed 7612 Harvard alumni (mean age 66.6 years) from 1988 through 1993, during which 366 cases of incident prostate cancer occurred.

effect_size.excerpt: Compared to men reporting almost never drinking alcohol in 1988, the multivariate relative risks (95% CI) for 1 drink/month to < 3 drinks/week, 3 drinks/week to < 1 drink/ day, 1 to < 3 drinks/day, and > or = 3 drinks/day were 1.33 (0.88-2.01), 1.65 (1.12-2.44), 1.85 (1.29-2.64), and 1.33 (0.86-2.05), respectively. Wine or beer consumption was unassociated with prostate cancer; however, moderate liquor consumption was associated with a significant 61-67% increased risk of prostate cancer (P, non-linear trend < 0.001).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Compared to men reporting almost never drinking alcohol in 1988, the multivariate relative risks (95% CI) for 1 drink/month to < 3 drinks/week, 3 drinks/week to < 1 drink/ day, 1 to < 3 drinks/day, and > or = 3 drinks/day were 1.33 (0.88-2.01), 1.65 (1.12-2.44), 1.85 (1.29-2.64), and 1.33 (0.86-2.05), respectively.

comparison.excerpt: Compared to men reporting almost never drinking alcohol in 1988

exposure_measurement.excerpt: Self-reported alcohol consumption was assessed at baseline from wine, beer, and liquor intake.

extraction.p_value_method: two-sided Wald test from effect and 95% CI on the log scale
